lessons.statement: when the pilot fails to hold directional control in landing and the airplane veers or ground loops, the first code is usually loss of control on ground, but it divides between the landing-roll phase, the flare or touchdown phase, and the unspecified landing phase, and occasionally the generic landing loss of control in flight code or an abnormal runway contact in the flare, while directional control and aircraft control findings are flagged nearly every time.
lessons.scope: the phase the narrative gives decides the code: loss after the wheels are down and rolling points to the landing roll code, loss at the moment of flare or touchdown points to the flare or touchdown code, a bare mention of landing points to the generic landing ground code, a cause worded as losing directional control during the flare without describing a veer can be coded as an abnormal runway contact, and a narrative that treats the upset as airborne points to the generic landing loss of control in flight code, with a student pilot variant of the aircraft control finding when a student was flying.

lessons.statement: when the cause is the pilot's improper flare or poor recovery from a bounced landing, the NTSB most often codes a hard landing in the flare phase first, with abnormal runway contact or a loss of control on the ground as the next most common starts, and flags pilot aircraft control together with a landing flare or other performance item.
lessons.scope: an improper flare or bounce with a described touchdown points to the flare-phase hard landing code, rough contact without a hard landing description points to abnormal runway contact, a veer or swerve after touchdown points to loss of control on ground in the flare or landing roll phase, and a general-landing-phase hard landing code is used when the touchdown phase is not described, usually followed by a nose over, runway excursion or gear collapse, with an incorrect action finding only occasionally added when the narrative stresses the pilot's recovery technique.

lessons.statement: when the pilot fails to hold airspeed or pitch control and the airplane stalls, the NTSB flags a performance or control parameter finding with a pilot aircraft control finding, and the first code is aerodynamic stall or loss of control in flight in whichever phase the narrative places the stall, such as initial climb, low-altitude manoeuvring, the landing or a go-around, unless the narrative opens with a missed landing area, in which case an undershoot or overshoot comes first.
lessons.scope: the first code is stall or loss of control in flight in the phase of flight where the stall happens, including takeoff, initial climb, manoeuvring, low-altitude flying, landing and go-around, and it is an undershoot or overshoot code only when the narrative starts with a badly flown approach to the landing area; the pilot aircraft control finding is nearly constant, the airspeed or pitch control finding is usual, a delayed action or incorrect action finding is added only when the timing or the recovery is blamed, and an experience finding is added only when the narrative cites it.

lessons.statement: when a pilot loses directional control on the runway or taxiway in gusty or crosswind conditions, the first code is usually the loss of control on ground code for the phase, followed by a runway excursion, a nose over or other damage codes, and the findings flag pilot aircraft control and a performance or control parameter item, with a wind item added only when the narrative names the wind as a contributing factor or as something the pilot had to compensate for.
lessons.scope: the phase decides the first code, with the landing roll, the generic landing, the flare or touchdown, the takeoff run and taxi each having their own loss of control on ground code, while a narrative that describes the aircraft as airborne gives a loss of control in flight code and a narrative centered on a nose over may lead with the nose over code instead; the directional control or crosswind correction item is not always flagged and may appear as a general control parameter item, and the wind item is gusts, crosswind or general wind depending on what the narrative names.

lessons.statement: when the pilot or a student recovers badly from a bounced landing, the NTSB leads with a flare-phase runway code, hard landing or abnormal runway contact in about equal measure, less often loss of control on ground, and usually pairs a landing flare performance finding with an aircraft control finding.
lessons.scope: a lead that stresses the firm contact after the bounce points to the hard landing code, usually in the flare phase and sometimes the generic landing phase, a lead that stresses the bounce or the rebound itself points to the abnormal runway contact code, usually in the flare phase and sometimes the generic landing phase, and a lead on the veer or ground loop after the bounce points to the loss of control on ground code in the flare phase; follow-on codes such as loss of control on ground, runway excursion, nose over or collision with terrain or an object are common, the landing flare finding and the aircraft control finding on the pilot or student usually appear together but either may be missing, and an incorrect action finding or a delayed action finding on the pilot or instructor is only sometimes added when the recovery itself or a slow takeover is blamed.

lessons.statement: when the pilot is blamed for failing to maintain directional control or for inadequate compensation in crosswind or gusty wind during landing, the NTSB flags a pilot aircraft control finding, usually with a directional or crosswind control performance finding, adds a wind finding mainly when the cause speaks of compensation or names the wind as contributing, and the first code divides between loss of control on ground in the landing roll, loss of control on ground in the flare, loss of control in flight in the flare, and loss of control on ground with no landing phase given.
lessons.scope: the narrative phase decides the code: a veer after the wheels are rolling points most often to the landing roll loss of control on ground code, often followed by a runway excursion, nose over or other weather encounter, a veer at flare or touchdown points to the flare loss of control on ground code, a narrative that only says the pilot lost control in wind without describing ground handling can be coded as loss of control in flight in the flare, a landing described without a roll or flare phase can get the general landing loss of control on ground code, and a cause that speaks of directional control rather than compensation or wind often carries no wind finding.

lessons.statement: when a pilot's lack of experience is named as contributing, the NTSB flags an experience and qualifications finding, and the specific item depends on whether the narrative blames overall flight time, time in that make and model, or lack of recent flying.
lessons.scope: read the narrative for total experience, experience with the equipment type including unusual aircraft such as trikes, or recency of experience, and the experience finding is typically paired with a pilot aircraft control finding and never leads the cause.

lessons.statement: when the pilot fails to hold airspeed on the approach or landing, the NTSB flags an airspeed performance finding with a pilot aircraft control finding, and the first occurrence is most often a loss of control in flight or an aerodynamic stall in the pattern final or go-around phase, but it is a landing-phase stall, undershoot, overshoot, runway excursion or abnormal runway contact when the narrative stresses that outcome or the arrival point.
lessons.scope: the first code is loss of control in flight or an aerodynamic stall in pattern final or go-around when the narrative describes the airplane losing control or stalling while still in the pattern, usually followed by a collision with terrain; a stall in the flare, takeoff or generic landing phase when the narrative places the stall there; an undershoot or overshoot when it stresses the missed touchdown point; an abnormal runway contact or runway excursion when it stresses the contact or the roll-out; and a hard landing, wind or turbulence usually appears later in the chain rather than first.

lessons.statement: when the narrative names the pilot as impaired or incapacitated by alcohol, a drug or medication, or a lack of oxygen, the NTSB flags a pilot impairment finding whose specific item matches the substance or cause, while a deteriorated health condition or fatigue is coded as its own physical finding instead.
lessons.scope: applies when the cause or contributing factors cite impairment, incapacitation or hypoxia; the first occurrence depends on the phase of flight and is not predictable, and the pilot aircraft control and decision findings are common but not reliable here, while a health condition with no impairment wording or simple fatigue does not get the impairment finding.

lessons.statement: when a pilot fails to hold airspeed on approach or landing, the NTSB flags an airspeed not maintained finding together with a pilot aircraft control finding, and the first occurrence follows the phase the narrative places the event in, an aerodynamic stall in that phase when a stall is named, otherwise loss of control, an undershoot, a runway excursion or a collision on final.
lessons.scope: applies to airspeed lapses during pattern, instrument or landing phases of flight, where a named stall is coded as aerodynamic stall in the phase described (base, final, instrument final, flare or touchdown, or landing), an unnamed upset points to loss of control, a narrative that goes straight to ground contact points to the collision on final code, a short touchdown points to undershoot and is often followed by hard landing or a runway excursion, and a wind response finding is added only when wind or gusts are blamed.

lessons.statement: when the pilot fails to maintain airspeed and the airplane stalls during takeoff or the initial climb, the first code is loss of control in flight or an aerodynamic stall in the takeoff or initial climb phase, with an airspeed not maintained finding and usually an aircraft control finding, and a collision with terrain or an uncontrolled descent follows.
lessons.scope: applies to stalls from inadequate airspeed in the takeoff and initial climb phases only: the phase at the time of the upset picks the takeoff or initial climb code, and the loss of control code or the aerodynamic stall code comes first depending on whether the narrative treats the stall itself as the defining event, so low flying, maneuvering after a tow or power failure, and climb to cruise are not covered.

lessons.statement: when a flight instructor or examiner is blamed for reacting too late to take over from the pilot being instructed, the NTSB flags a delayed-action finding against the instructor, and the first occurrence follows the phase and event the narrative names, most often a flare hard landing or a loss of control on ground in the landing roll or at touchdown, but sometimes a landing code with no phase detail or a loss of control in another phase.
lessons.scope: applies to dual instruction or check flights where the cause names the instructor's late or inadequate remedial action; a firm touchdown or bounce in the flare leads with the flare hard landing code, a directional loss of control in the rollout leads with the landing roll loss of control on ground code, a veer at touchdown leads with the flare loss of control on ground code, a landing event the narrative does not place in a phase can lead with the unspecified landing hard landing or loss of control in flight code, and a problem on approach, go-around or takeoff leads with that phase's own code, with runway excursion, collision or post-impact codes following later and performance and aircraft control findings added for the pilot's handling.

lessons.statement: when the pilot is blamed for failing to maintain directional control or to compensate for crosswind or gusts during takeoff, the NTSB codes a takeoff loss of control first, on ground or in flight, and follows it with a runway excursion, a collision with terrain or objects or a nose over, together with performance and control parameter, aircraft control and wind findings.
lessons.scope: loss of control on ground leads when the run or veer on the runway is stressed, loss of control in flight leads when the cause speaks of lost control of the airplane after it left the ground or without naming the ground run, and a runway excursion or nose over leads only when the cause stresses the excursion or the tip-over itself; the follow-on codes are runway excursion, collision with terrain or objects, nose over or an other weather encounter when a gust is cited, and the findings are a directional or crosswind control item, an aircraft control item for the pilot, and a wind item chosen by whether the narrative names a crosswind or gusts.

lessons.statement: when a bird or other animal strike is the cause, the NTSB codes a bird hit in flight as the birdstrike event in whatever phase the aircraft was in, but codes a deer or other animal met on the runway during takeoff or landing as a runway incursion animal event in that phase, and in both cases flags an animal environmental finding rather than any pilot finding.
lessons.scope: applies when the strike itself is the cause; the phase code follows where the aircraft was when struck, birds struck while airborne get the birdstrike code, and ground animals on the runway during takeoff, landing or landing roll get the runway incursion animal code, sometimes followed by a collision, airport or off-field landing event.

lessons.statement: when the pilot is blamed for not compensating for gusting or crosswind conditions while landing, the NTSB flags a wind response finding with a pilot aircraft control finding, and the first code is loss of control in flight in whichever phase the upset is placed, which is the flare, the generic landing phase or final approach, unless the cause describes only a rough touchdown, in which case abnormal runway contact leads.
lessons.scope: loss of control in flight leads when the cause says the pilot lost control or directional control, with the flare version when the upset is at touchdown and the final approach version when it happens before the runway, abnormal runway contact leads when the cause only says the pilot failed to maintain control or compensate and the narrative describes a bounce or gear failure, and a performance parameter finding such as crosswind correction or directional control is added only when the cause names that control axis.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot lets airspeed decay and the airplane stalls, the NTSB codes the event in the phase of flight where it began, usually as a loss of control in flight followed by the aerodynamic stall or spin and then a collision with terrain, and flags an airspeed performance finding with pilot aircraft control.
pushed_out.scope: applies to stalls from decayed airspeed in maneuvering, low-altitude flying, initial climb or pattern flight, including turn-backs after a power problem, where a power loss or other malfunction is coded as its own event that may come before the stall, and an attempted-recovery code appears only when the recovery itself is described as a failure.

pushed_out.statement: when a dual instruction landing ends in a hard landing after the trainee flares or recovers badly, the NTSB codes the instructor's delayed or missing remedial action as a personnel action finding together with an aircraft performance and control finding for the trainee's flare.
pushed_out.scope: applies to dual instruction landings where the trainee flares or recovers from a bounce improperly and the instructor does not take over in time, so the first event is a hard landing in the flare, and not to simulated emergencies, stalls or autorotations, which start with other events.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot fails to maintain directional control during the takeoff run, the NTSB flags directional control not maintained together with pilot aircraft control or an incorrect action finding, and the first code divides between takeoff loss of control on ground, takeoff loss of control in flight, a takeoff runway excursion and a collision with terrain or an object in the takeoff phase, with the nose over or later excursion usually coded after the lead.
pushed_out.scope: the lead is loss of control on ground when the narrative describes a veer or loss of directional control on the runway, a collision with terrain or an object when the narrative stresses the impact, a runway excursion when the cause is worded only as leaving the runway, loss of control in flight when the narrative describes a general loss of control in crosswinds or after liftoff, and a dynamic rollover code leads for a helicopter that rolls over after losing control, with a crosswind or surface environmental finding added when the wind or surface is named as contributing and a general control not maintained finding in place of the directional one when the cause says only control was lost.

pushed_out.statement: when the cause is a failure to hold the proper glide path on final approach, the NTSB reliably flags a descent, approach and glide path finding under aircraft performance, but the first occurrence code splits between a landing collision with terrain or an object, a landing area undershoot, and other landing or approach events, depending on how the outcome is worded.
pushed_out.scope: the collision with terrain or object code leads when the cause names the thing struck or the short landing, the undershoot code leads when the cause is worded as an undershoot of the landing area, and a hard landing or an approach altitude deviation code leads when the cause stresses the touchdown or the approach itself, while the second pilot finding varies between aircraft control, decision making and action selection.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot fails to clear trees or other obstacles during the initial climb after takeoff, the NTSB most often codes a collision during takeoff or landing in the initial climb phase, sometimes controlled flight into terrain instead, and flags a pilot aircraft control or climb rate performance finding, adding light and terrain findings only when the narrative names them as contributing.
pushed_out.scope: applies to departures where the airplane did not climb enough to clear obstacles or rising terrain ahead; the collision code is typical when the narrative describes striking trees or objects, the controlled flight into terrain code is less common, and darkness or terrain findings appear only when named as contributing.

pushed_out.statement: when a helicopter pilot fails to keep main rotor speed adequate, the NTSB codes the first event by the phase in which the decay is met, most often an autorotation ending in a hard landing, and flags a rotor parameter not-maintained performance finding with a pilot aircraft control finding, adding instructor supervision or delayed action findings when a CFI was aboard.
pushed_out.scope: applies to helicopter accidents where the narrative cites inadequate rotor speed as the pilot's failure and names no mechanical or weather cause, including training flights; the low-altitude manoeuvring loss of lift code is only one possible first event, and approach, enroute, landing flare and autorotation phases take their own codes.

pushed_out.statement: when a practice or simulated helicopter autorotation ends in a hard landing, the first code is most often the autorotation-phase hard landing or loss of control in flight, but it shifts to a landing-flare or touchdown hard landing when the narrative centers on a poor flare or on failing to arrest the descent at the end, usually with a pilot aircraft control finding and a rotor or descent rate performance finding.
pushed_out.scope: a rotor speed not maintained, an improper recovery or an excessive sink rate in a practice autorotation points to an autorotation-phase hard landing or loss of control in flight, with an attempted-recovery or training-event code often following; a loss of lift or loss of tail rotor effectiveness code leads only when the narrative stresses lost rotor energy or an aggressive recovery from excess descent; an inadequate flare, a simulated engine-out touchdown or a hovering autorotation points to a landing-flare or touchdown code; an instructor who was slow to take over adds a delayed-action finding for the instructor, while the performance finding names what was not maintained, such as rotor parameters, descent rate or the flare.

pushed_out.statement: when an animal on the runway is struck during the landing roll, the flare or touchdown, or the takeoff run, the NTSB codes a runway incursion by an animal in that phase and flags an object or animal environmental finding rather than any pilot finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause is the collision with the animal itself and no pilot, mechanical or weather factor is named, the phase code follows where the aircraft was when the animal was struck, the landing versions are usually the only event while a takeoff version is followed by a collision with terrain or an object, and the finding item concerns the effect on the equipment or the pilot's ability to respond.

pushed_out.statement: when two aircraft collide because a pilot did not see the other, the NTSB codes a midair collision in the phase being flown, most often VFR pattern final, adds an uncontrolled descent collision with terrain when an aircraft then falls, and flags a monitoring-other-aircraft attention finding on the pilot and on the pilot of the other aircraft.
pushed_out.scope: applies to see-and-avoid midair collisions between two piloted aircraft, mainly in the traffic pattern or while maneuvering; the attention finding is coded for the other aircraft's pilot even when the cause names only one pilot, and a lack-of-action or traffic-pattern-procedure finding may be added.

pushed_out.statement: when a landing gear structural or attachment part fails under load during the landing roll and the cause sentence names only that part with no pilot or maintenance factor, the NTSB leads with a landing gear collapse in the landing roll phase and flags a landing gear system finding, with no reliable second code.
pushed_out.scope: applies only when the gear gives way on the landing roll; a collapse during taxi, takeoff, approach or flare or touchdown, a wheel failure coded as aircraft structural failure, a selector or extension system fault, or a cause that cites maintenance or lubrication does not follow it, and a narrative led by the pilot's loss of directional control belongs to the gear-fault directional control pattern.

pushed_out.statement: when the cause blames water or debris in the fuel itself for a power loss, the NTSB leads with a fuel contamination code in the phase where power was lost, usually follows with the off-field landing and a terrain collision, and flags a fuel fluid condition finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies only when the cause names contaminated fuel as the sole reason for the power loss, with no wrong fuel serviced, no damaged or degraded fuel system component such as a strainer or carburetor part, and no pilot or maintenance factor; it does not apply when a component is blamed (coded as fuel starvation with a fuel system finding), when the wrong fuel was loaded, or when maintenance or ground crew are faulted, and the phase code follows where the aircraft was when power was lost.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot is blamed for failing to keep control of a glider during a tow launch, the NTSB flags a pilot aircraft control finding together with a performance and control parameters finding, and the first occurrence is a takeoff-phase code if the trouble comes during the launch roll but the initial climb glider tow event code if it comes after liftoff.
pushed_out.scope: a narrative about the launch roll or aero-tow start points to the takeoff glider tow event or takeoff loss of control code, a narrative about a release or line failure at low height after liftoff points to the initial climb glider tow event code, and a tow equipment finding is added only when the equipment itself failed, was misused or was overloaded.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot is blamed for failing to maintain control during the approach, the NTSB leads with loss of control in flight coded to the specific approach or landing phase, usually adds a collision with terrain or an uncontrolled descent, and flags the pilot aircraft control finding together with an aircraft performance and control parameter finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause names a failure to maintain control on approach, whether in the pattern, on an instrument final or on the landing approach, and the phase code follows where the flight was when control was lost, with any weather, airspeed or experience factor adding further findings.

pushed_out.statement: when both pilots are blamed for failing to see and avoid each other and their aircraft collide, the NTSB codes a midair collision as the first event, with the phase set by where the aircraft met, and flags an attention and monitoring finding, usually monitoring of other aircraft, once against each pilot.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the stated cause is a mutual failure to see and avoid, the phase of the midair code follows where the aircraft were when they met (traffic pattern final, initial climb, maneuvering or approach), and the attention finding is repeated for the pilot of each aircraft; the specific attention subcategory varies and a consequent event or a minor contributing factor may follow.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot fails to monitor terrain clearance during a visual descent at night and flies into rising ground, the NTSB codes a control flight into terrain event in the phase as the only occurrence and flags a monitoring of the environment finding against the pilot.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause is not watching or keeping clear of terrain with no weather entry, loss of control or mechanical factor named, and the phase code follows where the aircraft was when it struck the ground.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot fails to maintain directional control while taxiing with no wind or weather cause blamed and the event ends during the taxi without becoming a takeoff, the NTSB codes loss of control on ground in the general taxi phase first, followed by a collision with terrain or object, a dragged part or a roll over, and flags a directional control not-maintained finding with a pilot aircraft control finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to taxi veers in light aircraft including gyroplanes on rough or unfamiliar surfaces where the pilot simply lost heading control and the narrative names no gust, crosswind or shifting wind, no diverted attention, and no continuation into takeoff or flight; when wind is blamed, the taxi phase becomes a more specific segment such as to or from the runway, an other weather encounter occurrence and a wind finding are added, and when the taxi runs into a takeoff or an inadvertent liftoff the later in-flight or takeoff event can come first.

pushed_out.statement: when a helicopter pilot exceeds what the aircraft can deliver in thin air at low altitude in mountainous terrain, the NTSB flags a high density altitude finding in the temperature, humidity and pressure category, and it picks the first occurrence by the maneuver the narrative names: loss of control in flight for a general failure to stay within performance capabilities, low altitude operations for canyon or terrain flying that exceeds climb capability, and loss of lift for an out of ground effect hover or quick stop.
pushed_out.scope: applies to helicopter accidents where the narrative blames the pilot for exceeding aircraft capability in high density altitude conditions; the first occurrence follows the maneuver described, while the aircraft performance finding, the other contributing findings and the effect marker on the density altitude finding vary from case to case and are not predicted.

pushed_out.statement: when the cause says only that the landing gear collapsed for undetermined reasons, without naming which gear, side, component or system, the NTSB codes the collapse in its phase as the sole event and flags only a not-determined finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies only to the bare cause wording that the landing gear collapsed for undetermined reasons; once the sentence names a particular gear, side, strut, actuator or extension system, the NTSB usually adds a landing gear system finding for that part and often more events such as runway excursion, structural failure or loss of control, so this pattern does not carry over.

pushed_out.statement: when the narrative says the pilot's inadequate preflight or fuel planning, or failure to refuel, let the fuel run out, the NTSB codes a fuel exhaustion occurrence in whatever phase the power was lost (enroute, approach, pattern final, maneuvering or emergency descent), often followed by a total loss of power code, with a fuel planning or preflight inspection finding and a fluid level or fuel management finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the narrative attributes the power loss to fuel running out because fuel was not planned for or the airplane was not refuelled; the first occurrence is usually fuel exhaustion in the phase where power was lost, but a total loss of power code sometimes leads, and the personnel finding is fuel planning, preflight inspection or decision making depending on the wording, paired with a fuel level or fuel management finding.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot fails to keep clear of a wire, tree, crops or similar obstacle, the first code follows the phase, being low altitude operations for low manoeuvring, collision during takeoff or landing for takeoff and initial climb, and collision with terrain or object for approach, with a pilot attention or monitoring finding the most regular finding and object or altitude findings only sometimes added.
pushed_out.scope: this applies to obstacle strikes during low flying such as crop work or wire contact, during takeoff and the initial climb, and on approach or short final, where a later collision with terrain or object or an uncontrolled descent code may follow the first code, while a loss of engine power or a control loss leaves the first code to the power or control event.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot is blamed for spatial disorientation and then failing to keep control, the NTSB flags a perception, orientation or illusion finding, usually with an aircraft control or performance parameter finding, and leads with either loss of control in flight or, when the cause stresses flying from VFR into IMC, the VFR encounter with IMC, followed by the terrain collision.
pushed_out.scope: the lead is the loss of control in the phase where it began, whether initial climb, enroute, maneuvering or an instrument approach, unless the cause stresses the weather encounter, in which case that code leads; a decision, experience, fatigue or impairment finding is added only when the cause cites choosing to fly in IMC, lacking recent instrument time, being tired or being impaired, and a structural failure code appears only as a later event.

pushed_out.statement: when a landing gear component fails from fatigue, wear or corrosion and the pilot is not blamed, the NTSB opens with landing gear collapse in the landing roll if the gear gives way during the rollout, but opens with a component malfunction or a collapse in the flare and touchdown phase if it fails at touchdown, and in every case flags a landing gear system finding at the specific failed part, adding personnel or organizational findings only when inspection or design shortfalls are cited.
pushed_out.scope: applies to gear failures traced to age, wear or fatigue on a normal landing with no pilot fault, and the phase of the first occurrence follows when the gear gave way, while a collapse blamed on an earlier poor landing instead adds pilot and instructor findings.

pushed_out.statement: when a downdraft, windshear, updraft or sudden wind shift upsets the flight near the ground or in climb, the NTSB flags a wind environmental finding, and the first code divides between a windshear or thunderstorm encounter when the cause names the shear itself and a collision, hard landing or loss of control in that phase when the cause names the outcome, with an other weather encounter code usually following.
pushed_out.scope: the windshear code leads when the cause names windshear or a downdraft exceeding climb performance, mostly in initial climb, takeoff or enroute, and an aircraft capability finding appears only when the cause says capability was exceeded; the outcome code (collision, hard landing, loss of control or terrain collision) leads when the cause stresses what happened after the wind struck, as in go-arounds, landings, helicopters and balloons, with the phase code following where the aircraft was; pilot findings appear only when the narrative blames the pilot's decision or handling.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot simply fails to keep control during a low-altitude manoeuvre with no cause given, the NTSB usually leads with loss of control in flight in the manoeuvring phase, follows it with a collision with terrain or an uncontrolled descent collision, and flags a pilot aircraft control finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to low manoeuvring flights where the narrative names neither a mechanical problem, a weather problem nor an obstacle, and a cause that stresses an obstacle belongs to the obstacle-clearance patterns instead.

pushed_out.statement: when a landing gear leg or actuator fails or collapses during landing for reasons the investigation states as undetermined, the NTSB flags the failed landing gear component as the finding, usually with no pilot finding and only sometimes with a not-determined finding added, and the first occurrence is most often landing gear collapse in the landing roll but may instead be a structural failure, a system failure or a touchdown event.
pushed_out.scope: applies to nose or main gear collapses, actuator failures or uncommanded retractions at touchdown or in the landing roll where the cause is stated as undetermined and no wear, maintenance or pilot cause is identified; the finding names the failed component rather than a general not-determined item.

pushed_out.statement: when a fire of undetermined origin is the cause, the NTSB codes a non-impact fire or smoke event in the phase of flight where it occurred, adds later events such as an emergency descent, power loss or collision only if they actually followed, and flags only a not-determined finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause gives only a fire of undetermined origin and names no pilot, mechanical or weather factor, whether the fire occurred on the ground or in flight.

pushed_out.statement: when the cause names failure to maintain directional control on landing as the main factor and improper brake application only as a contributing one, the NTSB leads with loss of control on ground in the landing roll, sometimes followed by abnormal runway contact, and flags directional control, brake incorrect-use, pilot aircraft control and incorrect action findings.
pushed_out.scope: applies to landing rollouts where the cause puts directional control first and brake misuse second as a contributing factor and no mechanical brake fault is found, while causes that lead with excessive braking or excessive speed and end in a runway departure belong to the runway excursion pattern, and a braking-caused nose over belongs to the nose over pattern.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot fails to keep clear of terrain during a descent at night or in low cloud and fog, the NTSB defines the event as controlled flight into terrain in the descent phase, follows it with a post-impact fire, and flags an altitude not-maintained performance finding with a pilot attention finding for monitoring the environment.
pushed_out.scope: applies to descents into mountainous or rising terrain in poor visibility where no upset is described and no mechanical cause is blamed, and the weather or light condition is carried in the narrative rather than as a separate pilot finding.

pushed_out.statement: when a pilot continues an instrument approach below the published minimum descent altitude or decision height without the required visual references and hits terrain, water or obstacles short of the runway, the NTSB leads with a control flight into terrain code in the instrument final approach phase and flags decision making and action findings against the pilot, adding an altitude deviation or a weather encounter event as a second occurrence only when the cause stresses the altitude or the visibility.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause is descending below the published approach minimum in poor visibility on an instrument final approach, with no mechanical or loss of control factor named, and the approach is not a circling approach or a landing-phase touchdown short of the runway, where the NTSB uses other first codes.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot is blamed for poorly applying short-field takeoff procedures or configuration and the airplane cannot clear obstacles, the NTSB most often leads with a collision in the initial climb phase and flags a use of equipment or information finding against the pilot.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause is skipped or poorly applied handbook takeoff procedures or configuration, with no power loss, stall or control problem named as the lead event.

pushed_out.statement: when a downdraft or windshear in rising or mountainous terrain exceeds the airplane's climb ability, the NTSB flags a wind downdraft finding, a climb capability finding and sometimes a pilot decision finding, but the first code divides between loss of control in flight, collision during takeoff and windshear in the enroute phase.
pushed_out.scope: cruise-phase encounters that end in loss of control are coded as enroute loss of control, encounters right after departure are coded as a takeoff collision followed by another weather encounter, and a narrative that names the windshear or downdraft as the event itself points to the enroute windshear code followed by a terrain collision with only the capability and wind findings and no decision finding.

pushed_out.statement: when a helicopter pilot lets a dynamic rollover develop during a landing, the NTSB leads with the dynamic rollover code in the landing phase, often adds a second landing code such as loss of control in the flare, abnormal runway contact or roll over, and flags a pilot aircraft control finding, frequently paired with a performance or control parameters finding that names lateral or bank control when drift is the issue.
pushed_out.scope: applies only when the rollover occurs in the landing itself with no mechanical or weather factor named; rollovers during hover or taxi, after a precautionary landing, or in a rejected takeoff take the phase code of that moment instead, and the takeoff version is covered by the takeoff control lessons.

pushed_out.statement: when an instructor is blamed for inadequate supervision or a late recovery after a student loses airspeed or mishandles a stall in a training manoeuvre, the NTSB usually leads with the aerodynamic stall or spin in the manoeuvring phase, may add attempted recovery when the cause stresses the recovery, ends with an uncontrolled descent collision, and flags an airspeed or angle of attack performance finding plus instructor monitoring and delayed action findings.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause names the instructor's supervision or delayed recovery rather than a mechanical or weather factor; loss of control in flight leads only when the cause frames the lost airspeed as a loss of control, and a safety program finding is added only when the cause also criticizes the school's oversight.

pushed_out.statement: when the aircraft and pilot are missing and no cause can be found, the NTSB codes a missing aircraft event followed by a general unknown or undetermined code and flags only a not-determined finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to disappearances where no wreckage or evidence is available, so no pilot, aircraft or environmental finding can be flagged.

pushed_out.statement: when the cause sentence says only that an unknown event or undetermined reasons damaged the airplane and describes no resulting loss of control, landing or impact sequence, the NTSB codes a single unknown or undetermined occurrence and flags only a not-determined finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause attributes damage found on the airframe to an unknown event, names no pilot, weather or mechanical factor, and gives no phase of flight and no loss of control, vibration, landing, collision or rollover; it does not apply when the cause is a bare undetermined statement or describes an upset, landing or collision, because then the NTSB codes the phase and the resulting events and often adds specific findings.

pushed_out.statement: when a flight instructor is blamed in a student's landing or approach accident, the NTSB codes a monitoring-of-another-person attention finding for wording about inadequate supervision and a delayed action finding for wording about slow remedial action, using both only when the cause names both, with the student's or pilot's own aircraft control finding kept alongside.
pushed_out.scope: read the cause wording to see whether the instructor failed to supervise or intervened late, since supervision wording alone gives the monitoring finding and delayed remedial action wording alone gives the delayed action finding without a monitoring finding, while the first occurrence code follows the event in its phase and is not set by either instructor finding.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot is blamed for failing to attain the proper touchdown point, the NTSB usually leads with a landing area overshoot code, coded under either the general landing phase or the flare phase, and then adds a runway excursion or a collision, with the landing roll runway excursion code leading in some overruns and the undershoot code leading only when the airplane came down short of the runway.
pushed_out.scope: the overshoot code leads when the airplane touched down long or the pilot did not go around, followed by a runway excursion, a nose over, a loss of control on the ground or a collision, while the landing roll runway excursion code leads when the airplane ran off the runway without a separate overshoot code, and the undershoot code is rare and tied to a short arrival; the findings usually flag descent or approach path not attained together with aircraft control as a use of equipment or information issue, with lack of action or delayed action added when a go-around was not made.

pushed_out.statement: when the cause is a loss of control for undetermined reasons, the NTSB leads with the loss of control code for whatever phase the flight was in, mostly takeoff, initial climb, manoeuvring or cruise, and flags a not-determined finding, often paired with a performance and control parameter finding.
pushed_out.scope: the phase named in the narrative sets the first code, so takeoff, initial climb, manoeuvring and enroute cruise each take their own loss of control in flight code, a directional loss of control on the takeoff roll may take the loss of control on ground code, and a stall described as the event takes the aerodynamic stall code in that phase, with terrain collision, uncontrolled descent collision, post-impact fire or system malfunction codes often following, a bare impact with terrain for undetermined reasons leading with an unknown or undetermined code, and a personnel task performance finding for aircraft control added only when the cause names the pilot's failure to control the aircraft.

pushed_out.statement: when a pilot becomes spatially disoriented after flying into cloud, fog, darkness or reduced visibility, the NTSB's first code follows what the cause stresses, loss of control in flight when the cause is the disorientation and the lost control itself, and VFR encounter with IMC when the cause is the decision to depart or continue into the weather.
pushed_out.scope: a cause worded as failure to maintain control due to disorientation, in climb, initial climb, cruise or on an approach, gives loss of control in flight first, followed by an uncontrolled descent collision, with spatial disorientation and pilot aircraft control findings and sometimes only the disorientation finding, and a cause that blames the decision to take off or continue into weather without instrument qualification gives VFR encounter with IMC first, often followed by loss of visual reference, with a decision finding and a weather visibility finding, and the disorientation finding is often absent in these cases, although a low-level departure into fog can still start with the VFR encounter even when the cause names the disorientation.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot or student is slow to abandon a takeoff or misjudges the runway before departing and the airplane overruns, the NTSB flags a delayed-action finding, sometimes with a recognition finding, but the first code divides between a collision in the rejected-takeoff phase, a runway excursion in the rejected-takeoff phase, loss of control on ground in the takeoff phase, a runway excursion in the takeoff phase and a loss of lift in the takeoff phase.
pushed_out.scope: a narrative that treats the run as an abandoned takeoff points to the rejected-takeoff runway excursion code or to the rejected-takeoff collision code when the cause stresses hitting trees or objects on the ground, with a preflight or dispatch event and the excursion following, a narrative stressing the veer or loss of directional control during the run points to takeoff loss of control on ground followed by the runway excursion and an object collision, a narrative citing a heavy airplane that could not lift off may lead with the takeoff loss of lift code followed by the takeoff runway excursion and a rejected-takeoff collision, and a control or equipment malfunction that prompted the abort may be coded first as a flight control malfunction followed by an attempted-recovery code.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot lands with a tailwind, the NTSB usually opens with a landing roll event, either loss of control on ground or a runway excursion, and flags decision making, adding a tailwind wind finding when the wind is named.
pushed_out.scope: loss of control on ground leads when the cause is worded as losing directional control or an unstable approach, and runway excursion leads when the cause stresses an overrun or a long touchdown on a slick runway; the decision finding appears in both, with aircraft control and directional control findings added when the cause names a control failure; the first code moves to the flare phase for a bounced or hard landing, to a landing phase loss of control in flight for a stall, and to a takeoff collision when a touch-and-go is attempted.

pushed_out.statement: when a helicopter practice autorotation or other simulated emergency ends in a hard landing, the NTSB usually leads with hard landing coded in the autorotation phase for practice autorotations or in the landing phase for other simulated failures, often adds attempted remediation or a simulated training event, and flags a performance finding on descent rate, airspeed, flare or rotor parameters together with a personnel finding against the pilot or instructor for aircraft control, delayed or missing action, or poor monitoring.
pushed_out.scope: applies to helicopter training flights where a practice autorotation or simulated system failure leads directly to the hard contact; the lead occurrence may instead be abnormal runway contact, loss of control in flight or a pattern-phase loss of control when control is lost during the manoeuvre, rollover or ground resonance often follows, and the personnel finding falls on the instructor when the cause blames delayed or missing intervention.

pushed_out.statement: when a helicopter pilot or student mishandles an autorotation, whether by letting rotor speed decay, flaring improperly or acting late, the NTSB leads with a hard landing in the autorotation phase and flags pilot action or flare and rotor parameter findings with pilot aircraft control.
pushed_out.scope: applies to real and simulated autorotations where the cause blames rotor speed management, the flare technique or a delayed remedial action, a loss of control in flight or an off-field landing code may follow the lead, and the specific finding is a rotor or descent rate parameter, a landing flare item or a delayed or incorrect action item depending on the wording.

pushed_out.statement: when the narrative cites an overweight or out-of-limits loaded airplane in a takeoff or initial climb accident, the NTSB usually faults the pilot with a planning and preparation finding for weight and balance calculations or a decision making finding, often adds an aircraft capability finding for the exceeded weight, center of gravity or climb limit, and only rarely adds a loading handling finding, while the lead occurrence follows the accident outcome rather than the loading.
pushed_out.scope: applies to takeoff and initial climb accidents where an overweight or out-of-limits loading condition is cited in the probable cause, whether as a contributing item or alongside the pilot's own error, with lead occurrences such as loss of control in flight, collision during takeoff or landing, runway excursion or gear collapse.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot is blamed for choosing to fly low over rising terrain or in weather conducive to downdrafts or turbulence, the NTSB leads with the low altitude operations code in the low-altitude manoeuvring phase and flags a decision making finding against the pilot.
pushed_out.scope: the turbulence encounter, loss of control or terrain collision that follows is coded after the lead, a knowledge of weather or climb rate performance finding is added only when the narrative stresses them, and impairment from alcohol with a clearance failure while low also leads with the low altitude operations code with an impairment finding in place of the decision finding.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot's inadequate preflight inspection leaves the fuel supply unchecked and the engine quits in cruise, the NTSB leads with fuel starvation in cruise, follows it with a preflight event and total loss of engine power, and flags a pilot preflight inspection finding with an inadequate-inspection item on the fuel system.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the narrative blames the failure to verify fuel quantity or fuel system condition before flight, and a stall after the power loss is only a later code unless the cause opens with the airspeed failure.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot misjudges speed and altitude on the approach and the airplane comes down short of the intended landing area, the NTSB defines the event as a landing area undershoot in the generic landing phase, follows it with a collision during takeoff or landing, and flags a pilot aircraft control finding with a descent or glide path performance finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to ordinary approaches that end short with no mechanical or weather cause blamed, and a practice forced landing that ends short belongs to the flare-phase undershoot pattern instead.

pushed_out.statement: when the reason for a loss of control during takeoff stays undetermined, the NTSB usually leads with a takeoff-phase loss-of-control occurrence, in flight if the aircraft was airborne and on ground if not, flags a not-determined finding, and usually adds an aircraft performance and control parameters finding whose detail varies with the case.
pushed_out.scope: applies to takeoff upsets, including helicopter departures and aborted landings, where no mechanical or weather cause is identified; follow-on occurrences such as aerodynamic stall, collision with terrain or post-impact fire are added when the narrative describes them, and a stall soon after liftoff may instead lead as an initial climb unknown occurrence.

pushed_out.statement: when the airplane collides with a bird in flight, the NTSB defines the event as a birdstrike in that phase and flags only an environmental animal or bird finding marked as an effect on equipment, with no pilot finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to bird impacts in any phase of flight where the narrative blames the animal itself rather than the pilot's choices.

pushed_out.statement: when icing conditions or ice contamination figure in a loss of control accident, the NTSB nearly always flags a conducive-to-structural-icing environmental finding, often with a pilot decision finding, but the first occurrence code depends on the phase and narrative emphasis, being an icing encounter when the icing is the named event in the enroute or descent phase and a loss of control in flight when the stall follows a takeoff or manoeuvring departure.
pushed_out.scope: a narrative naming icing as the event in the enroute, cruise or descent phase points to the icing encounter code for that phase, followed by loss of control in flight or an uncontrolled descent collision, whereas a narrative stressing contamination or a stall after takeoff or in the initial climb points to loss of control in flight for the takeoff or manoeuvring phase, and an approach stall may list loss of control first with the icing encounter second; a pilot decision finding is added when the pilot chose to fly into known icing, and an aircraft control finding only when the narrative faults handling.

pushed_out.statement: when maintenance personnel are blamed for improperly securing or servicing a rotor or other component that then separates or fails in flight, the NTSB codes a non-power system or component malfunction in the phase where it happened as the lead event and flags an incorrect service or maintenance item on that component.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause names the maintenance work as the origin and no pilot action is blamed, with an organizational policy or procedure finding added when an inadequate inspection procedure after the work is cited.

pushed_out.statement: when a pilot loses control during cruise flight, the NTSB opens the event chain with loss of control in flight in the cruise phase and then codes what followed, such as a storm encounter, a visual flight encounter with IMC, a structural failure or an uncontrolled descent collision with terrain, and it flags the pilot's aircraft control or experience only when the narrative blames them.
pushed_out.scope: applies to cruise upsets in clouds, in storms, from spatial disorientation, in low-g maneuvers or with no stated cause, but not when the structure fails or a flight instrument fails first, since the NTSB then often leads with that failure or with a maneuvering or emergency descent phase.

pushed_out.statement: when a failed carburetor or fuel control component causes the engine to lose power and no pilot action is blamed, the NTSB leads with a loss of engine power code in the phase where it happened, total or partial as described, follows with an off-field landing and a terrain collision, and flags only a damaged or degraded fuel control or carburetor finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause names the cracked, worn or malfunctioning carburetor part as the origin with no maintenance, pilot or weather factor, and it differs from ice in the carburetor, which carries an environmental finding, and from internal engine part failures, which carry an engine section finding.

pushed_out.statement: when a pilot fails to keep clear of terrain while manoeuvring in a canyon or similar confined terrain and no reason is established, the NTSB codes a collision with terrain or object under an unknown phase and flags a not-determined finding with an altitude not-maintained performance finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to terrain contact cases where the phase of flight is not specified by the narrative and no upset, mechanical or weather cause is described.

pushed_out.statement: when a pilot gets out of an airplane or helicopter with the engine still running and it moves away unattended, the first code is usually the operating-phase loss of control on ground or the operating miscellaneous code, followed by a ground collision or rollover, with a parking and securing finding and a pilot decision or action finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to a pilot who exits with the engine running, especially leaving a helicopter's collective unsecured, in gusty wind, or leaving a passenger near the throttle; the first code is the operating loss of control on ground code if the machine drives off and the operating miscellaneous code if it is coded as an unattended event, and some cases are coded instead as prior to flight or post-impact; it does not cover starts that get away from a pilot who is still at the controls, which are coded inconsistently between the start-up loss of control and ground collision codes.

pushed_out.statement: when a pilot fails to keep control during an aborted takeoff, the NTSB codes two rejected-takeoff events, one a runway excursion and the other a rejected-takeoff loss of control, and flags pilot aircraft control, with the order of the two varying.
pushed_out.scope: a cause that blames unexplained loss of directional control puts the runway excursion first with loss of control on ground second, a cause that blames failure to maintain control puts a rejected-takeoff loss of control code first with the runway excursion following, and the aircraft performance and control parameters finding is added only when the cause says control was not maintained.

pushed_out.statement: when a dual practice or simulated forced landing ends in a collision during the approach, the NTSB usually places the event in the VFR pattern final or go-around phase instead of a landing flare undershoot, often adds a simulated training event, and flags a glide path performance finding together with a delayed-action instructor finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to dual instructional flights where the probable cause cites the pilot's poor glide path or touchdown point and the instructor's delayed remedial action or late go-around; it does not apply when the event is coded as a landing flare undershoot.

pushed_out.statement: when a flight control is left improperly installed or unsecured and the pilot's inadequate preflight inspection is causal, the NTSB usually leads with loss of control in flight in the takeoff or climb phase, often ends with uncontrolled descent and collision with terrain, and flags a pilot preflight inspection finding alongside an incorrect service finding on whichever control system or surface was affected, without reliably coding a separate preflight event or flight control malfunction.
pushed_out.scope: applies to aircraft the pilot assembled, reinstalled or accepted after work with an unsecured control linkage, and when a mechanic's faulty work is also causal the lead may instead become a flight control malfunction in the climb, while the incorrect service finding may fall on structure rather than the flight control system.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot waits too long to abandon a landing and the airplane rolls over, the NTSB leads with a roll over in the landing phase and flags only a delayed-action finding against the pilot.
pushed_out.scope: applies to late decisions to go around where the narrative blames the timing of the decision rather than the handling, and no aircraft or environmental finding is flagged.

pushed_out.statement: when a landing gear leg collapses and the NTSB blames a poorly executed flare in wind, it codes only landing gear collapse in the landing roll and flags only a general task performance finding against the pilot.
pushed_out.scope: applies to landings where the narrative blames the pilot's technique rather than any gear defect, and no aircraft or environmental finding is flagged even though wind is mentioned.

pushed_out.statement: when a pilot who becomes lost keeps flying until the tanks run dry, the NTSB leads with a fuel exhaustion occurrence, ends with a collision with terrain or an object at touchdown, and flags a fuel level finding together with a geographic disorientation finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to pilots who lose their position and fly on until the fuel is gone; the lead fuel exhaustion occurrence is usually coded in cruise but can be coded during an emergency descent, and a fatigue finding is added only when the pilot reports being tired.

pushed_out.statement: when a propeller blade fails and separates in cruise and the report gives no cause, the NTSB codes part separation then total loss of engine power with a propeller blade failure finding and a not-determined finding, but if the pilot then loses control or maneuvers to a forced landing it instead leads with a powerplant or system malfunction, adds loss of control, and flags a pilot control or performance finding with no not-determined finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to in-flight propeller blade failures with no identified maintenance, fatigue or overload cause, where the not-determined pattern holds only when the flight ends in engine power loss without a later loss of control.

pushed_out.statement: when turbulence upsets the airplane and the NTSB blames the pilot or instructor for not regaining control, it leads with loss of control in flight in the phase flown, follows it with a turbulence encounter and an uncontrolled descent collision, and flags a general not-maintained performance finding with an aircraft control finding against the person flying.
pushed_out.scope: applies to turbulence upsets where the cause is the failure to recover rather than the atmosphere itself, so no turbulence environmental finding is flagged, and the aircraft control item names the instructor when one was flying.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot skips the manufacturer checklist and leaves trim or engine controls wrongly set so that directional control is lost soon after liftoff, the NTSB codes loss of control in flight in the initial climb, followed by an uncontrolled descent collision, and flags a directional control performance finding with preflight inspection and checklist-use findings against the pilot.
pushed_out.scope: applies to departures where the narrative blames the incomplete preflight and checklist rather than the handling alone, and the specific control left misset is named in the narrative rather than carried as a separate aircraft finding.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot descends below the published minimum altitudes during an instrument approach because of poor planning and strikes terrain, the NTSB defines the event as controlled flight into terrain in the instrument approach phase and flags a flight planning finding with an altitude not-maintained performance finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to instrument approaches flown without upset where no mechanical or weather cause is blamed, and a medication or impairment finding is added only when the narrative names it as contributing.

pushed_out.statement: when turbulence beyond what a light aircraft can handle upsets the flight, the NTSB leads with the turbulence encounter code in the phase where it happened, follows with a descent into terrain, and flags a turbulence environmental finding with an aircraft capability exceeded finding rather than a pilot finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause is the turbulence itself exceeding the performance limit of a light or ultralight type, and the specific turbulence item, such as clear air turbulence, follows what the narrative names.

pushed_out.statement: when a passenger is blamed for not bracing for the landing, the NTSB codes a miscellaneous event in the landing phase as the only occurrence and flags a lack-of-action finding against the passenger rather than the pilot.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause names only the passenger's failure to prepare for the touchdown and no pilot, mechanical or weather factor is cited.

pushed_out.statement: when the airplane meets an unseen hole or rough spot in the runway surface during the landing roll and no pilot handling is blamed, the NTSB codes an airport occurrence first, then a collision with terrain or an object, and flags only a rough terrain environmental finding about the effect on the operation.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause is the surface defect itself with no pilot, mechanical or weather factor named, and the phase code follows where the airplane was when the surface was struck.

pushed_out.statement: when maintenance personnel are blamed for a loose fuel line fitting that leads to an in-flight fire, the NTSB codes a non-impact fire or smoke event in the phase where it happened and flags a maintenance finding against the technicians with fastener and maintenance check items on the aircraft side.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause names the incorrectly tightened or installed fitting as the origin with no pilot action, weather or engine failure named, and the phase code follows where the aircraft was when the fire began.

pushed_out.statement: when a student's poor drift or skid-clearance control during a helicopter hover is blamed together with the instructor's inadequate supervision, the NTSB leads with a collision with terrain or an object in the hover phase rather than a rollover code and flags an instructor delayed-action finding with the student's aircraft control finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to dual hover training that ends in a rollover with no mechanical or weather factor named, a hover altitude or height performance finding may be added, and it differs from the pattern where only the instructor is blamed and the rollover code leads.

pushed_out.statement: when a defect introduced in manufacture causes an engine accessory or component to fail in flight, the NTSB leads with the loss of engine power in the phase where it happened, follows with the resulting landing event, and flags an engine section finding and a fuel or control component finding with a manufacturing finding against the maker rather than any pilot finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause is a contaminated or faulty part from production with no maintenance, pilot or weather factor named, the total or partial power code follows what the narrative says the engine kept producing, and the component items are damaged or degraded wording.

pushed_out.statement: when a pilot is struck by or walks into a turning propeller during start-up or ground handling, the NTSB codes aircraft or propeller contact with a person in the standing start-up phase and flags only a pilot attention finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to inadvertent encounters with a rotating propeller where no mechanical or environmental cause is blamed, and the cause is the pilot's lack of attention to the propeller.

pushed_out.statement: when the wings or other primary structure fail in cruise because of a design weakness such as flutter, the NTSB leads with an aircraft structural failure in the cruise phase, follows it with loss of control in flight and an uncontrolled descent collision, and flags only structures failure and design findings with no pilot finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to in-flight breakups blamed on inadequate stiffness or missing balance weights rather than on the pilot's handling, and the structures items name the failed component and carry both a failure item and a design item.

pushed_out.statement: when a rotor head or similar rotating part separates in flight because of fatigue from a defective manufacturing process, the NTSB leads with a non-power component malfunction in the phase flown, follows it with a part separation from the aircraft and an uncontrolled descent collision, and flags a rotor system fatigue finding with a manufacturer finding and no pilot finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to helicopter cruise breakups traced to a production flaw rather than to wear, maintenance or the pilot's handling, and the rotor item names the failed rotor component.

pushed_out.statement: when a fire starts in the engine area of a parked airplane and investigators cannot find its source, the NTSB codes a non-impact fire or smoke event in the standing phase with the engine not operating and flags only a not-determined finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to ground fires with no pilot, maintenance or mechanical cause identified, so no personnel or aircraft finding is flagged.

pushed_out.statement: when a pilot starts or continues a flight into known icing in an airplane not equipped for it, the NTSB flags a decision making finding with a structural icing weather finding and an aircraft capability exceeded finding, and codes the terrain or object collision as the only event.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause is the choice to fly into icing conditions beyond what the airplane can handle, with no mechanical or control problem named, and the phase code follows where the aircraft was when it came down.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot raises the landing gear too early after liftoff and the airplane settles back onto the runway, the NTSB codes a landing gear collapse in the takeoff phase and flags only an incorrect action finding against the pilot.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause is the timing of the retraction, with no equipment fault, weather or control problem named, and the gear system itself is not flagged.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot takes no corrective action as the aircraft loses altitude at low height and ends up in a forced landing on bad ground, the NTSB leads with a loss of lift code in the low-altitude manoeuvring phase, follows with an uncontrolled descent collision, and flags only a lack-of-action finding against the pilot.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause stresses the missing remedial action after the loss of altitude rather than a loss of control, stall or power problem, and the unsuitable terrain is the consequence rather than a separate decision finding.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot fails to hold directional control during a water landing in a float-equipped aircraft, the NTSB codes a dragged float or wing event in the flare or touchdown phase rather than loss of control on ground and flags a directional control performance finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause is directional control lost on the water surface with no weather, mechanical or other pilot finding named, and the aircraft control finding on the pilot is not always added.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot uses improper engine starting procedures and the airplane moves into another aircraft or object, the NTSB codes a ground collision in the engine operating phase and flags a procedure-use finding against the pilot.
pushed_out.scope: applies when no mechanical fault is named and the airplane is already running, which differs from the engine start-up phase patterns where excess power or an unsecured propped airplane is blamed.

pushed_out.statement: when a non-instrument pilot is blamed for spatial disorientation in darkness or over water and the airplane hits the surface, the NTSB codes loss of visual reference in the manoeuvring phase as the only event and flags only a perception, orientation or illusion finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause names the disorientation and the poor visibility conditions without blaming a decision to continue into weather or a later loss of control, which otherwise leads to the loss of control in flight pattern.

pushed_out.statement: when a throttle or power lever malfunctions during landing for an unknown reason and the airplane overruns, the NTSB codes a powerplant component malfunction in the landing roll first, then a runway excursion and an object collision, and flags an engine controls malfunction finding with a not-determined finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause names the failed control and no pilot action, maintenance or weather factor is blamed, and the phase code follows where the aircraft was when the control failed.

pushed_out.statement: when the cause is a pilot's inadvertent encounter with rotor downwash or other blast from another aircraft on the ground, the NTSB codes a prop, jet or rotor blast event in the engine operating phase as the only occurrence and flags a wake turbulence environmental finding about its effect on the equipment rather than a pilot finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause is the blast or downwash itself with no pilot handling, mechanical or weather factor named, and the phase is the standing engine operating phase.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot loses directional control while trying to avoid an animal on the runway during the landing rollout, the NTSB codes loss of control on ground in the landing roll rather than an animal runway incursion and flags a directional control performance finding with an animal environmental finding about its effect on the operation.
pushed_out.scope: applies when the cause is the pilot's loss of control during the evasive manoeuvre rather than a strike, which differs from the animal strike pattern that carries no pilot finding, and the pilot aircraft control finding is not always added.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot takes off too close behind a large aircraft and meets its wake, the NTSB defines the event as a takeoff wake turbulence encounter, follows it with loss of control on ground and a runway excursion, and flags only a pilot identification or recognition decision finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to departures behind heavier aircraft where separation was inadequate, and no aircraft or environmental finding is flagged because the cause is the pilot's failure to recognise and avoid the wake.

pushed_out.statement: when an engine fails or burns just after takeoff and the pilot mishandles the emergency return, the NTSB leads with a power plant malfunction in the takeoff phase, follows it with fire or smoke and a loss of control in the emergency descent, and flags a pilot aircraft control finding with an incorrect-use engine control item and a power plant malfunction item.
pushed_out.scope: applies to emergency returns where the pilot is blamed for failing to secure the failed engine or hold control, and the fire is treated as contributing when its origin is undetermined.

pushed_out.statement: when the crew lets airspeed decay while manoeuvring during a simulated engine failure, the NTSB leads with an aerodynamic stall in the low-altitude manoeuvring phase, follows it with a simulated training event and an uncontrolled descent collision, and flags an airspeed performance finding with a lack-of-action finding against the crew.
pushed_out.scope: applies to training flights where the stall comes from the practice emergency itself rather than from a real power loss.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot starts a takeoff while vehicles or other aircraft are operating on the runway and strikes one, the NTSB codes a ground collision in the takeoff phase and flags only a pilot decision making finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to departures into an occupied runway where the cause is the choice to go despite the traffic, and no aircraft or environmental finding is flagged.

pushed_out.statement: when turbulence or a dust devil upsets the airplane shortly after departure and no pilot error is blamed, the NTSB codes loss of control in flight in the initial climb, follows it with a turbulence encounter and an uncontrolled descent collision, and flags only environmental turbulence and wind findings marked as an effect on operation.
pushed_out.scope: applies to upsets blamed on the atmosphere itself rather than on the pilot's handling, and no personnel finding is flagged.

pushed_out.statement: when a pilot makes an abrupt manoeuvre to avoid another aircraft and then loses control, the NTSB leads with the abrupt manoeuvre in the phase flown, follows it with loss of control in flight and a terrain collision, and flags a monitoring-other-aircraft attention finding against both pilots with a pilot aircraft control finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to traffic pattern and climb conflicts where the evasive action leads to an airspeed or lift problem, and the performance item is airspeed not maintained when the narrative stresses the lost airspeed.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot underestimates the distance needed to clear obstructions on a takeoff from an unprepared strip such as a road, the NTSB codes a collision during takeoff, often followed by a nose over, and flags a takeoff distance capability finding with a pilot decision making finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to departures from roads or short strips where the narrative blames misjudged takeoff distance rather than a power or weather problem, and the obstruction struck is not itself flagged.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot turns off the runway at excessive speed and hits something, the NTSB codes a ground collision in the landing roll phase and flags a pilot decision making finding with a surface speed or braking performance finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to exits from the runway after touchdown where the narrative blames speed on the turn rather than a mechanical or surface cause.

pushed_out.statement: when the pilot fails to keep clear of terrain during aerobatics and investigators cannot establish why, the NTSB codes a collision with terrain or object in the aerobatics phase and flags only a not-determined finding.
pushed_out.scope: applies to aerobatic flights where the narrative names the failed clearance but no cause for it, so no pilot, aircraft or environmental finding beyond not determined is flagged.

pushed_out.statement: when the cause names only poor preflight planning that led to a tailwind takeoff and says nothing of degraded climb or a decision to depart downwind, the NTSB codes a collision during takeoff and flags only a flight planning finding, whereas a cause stressing poor climb performance or a faulty wind decision adds climb capability and decision findings.
pushed_out.scope: applies to tailwind departures where the narrative cause is limited to the planning failure and no aircraft performance, airspeed, equipment or decision finding is flagged; it does not hold when the cause cites degraded climb capability, misjudged wind change or flap use.

pushed_out.statement: when a faulty ignition component lets the engine start unexpectedly while someone turns the propeller by hand and the pilot is not blamed, the NTSB leads with an electrical system malfunction before flight, follows it with a ground handling event, and flags only an ignition system finding for the damaged part.
pushed_out.scope: applies to hand-turning of the propeller on the ground where a broken or degraded ignition lead or magneto grounding wire is the cause, and the ignition item names the failed component rather than any pilot action.
